clue.text: Leave off part of song

definitions.meaning: to stop doing a thing, or to hold back from starting it
the lines that come round again unchanged after every verse

explanation.surface: Somebody told to cut a section out of the number they are singing.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves run together into one plausible instruction about a song, so there is nothing to mark where the first definition stops. One is a verb, the other a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To refrain is to hold back from an action; a refrain is the chorus a song keeps returning to, so both halves land on the same word.

clue.text: Unreliable film about boxing

definitions.meaning: wobbly and liable to give way, said of a table, a marriage or a business
the 1976 picture in which Sylvester Stallone's club fighter gets a shot at the world title

explanation.surface: A shaky movie about the fight game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' sits in the middle looking like a container instruction and is only the preposition it appears to be. A title can define a common adjective when the title is that adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rocky is unsteady and cannot be counted on, and Rocky is also the name of the boxing film, so the second half names it outright.

clue.text: Basically supply name, first to last, and score

indicators.note: The letter standing first is sent round to the end, and the others close up in front of it keeping their order.

parts.note: to supply the money for a thing is to fund it
NAME with its leading N carried round to the back
a running score kept by strokes on a sheet is a tally

explanation.surface: An instruction to hand over your name in full and then settle up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First to last' reads as 'from beginning to end' in the surface, which is why the rotation hides inside it. 'Score' here is a count of points, not a piece of music.
explanation.definitionFit: What is fundamentally so is so at the foundation, which is the claim 'basically' makes in plainer words.

clue.text: Expert wearing a new protective garment

indicators.note: What you wear goes round you, so the expert named before the word is written inside the letters that follow.

parts.note: the article taken as itself
a pro is the professional, the expert as against the amateur
n is the standard short form of new

explanation.surface: A specialist trying on something freshly bought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A new' looks like an adjective waiting for its noun and is really two separate letters with a gap between them. Wearing puts the wearer inside the clothing, not the other way about.
explanation.definitionFit: An apron is tied on over your clothes to keep the cooking or the sawdust off them, so it protects rather than merely covers.

clue.text: A study written up about Virginia, US state

indicators.note: In a down clue what is written up runs from the foot of the entry towards the top, so those letters go in backwards.
Set about a thing means placed round the outside of it, so the letters made so far close over what follows.

parts.note: a study is a den, so A and DEN make four letters and the climb turns them round
VA is the two-letter postal code for Virginia

explanation.surface: Notes about a woman called Virginia, written up in the quiet of the study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A study' is two pieces of wordplay glued into one noun phrase, and a bare A is the easiest letter in a clue to read straight past. Virginia is a woman's name in the surface and a postal code in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Nevada is the desert state between California and Utah, so 'US state' names it by its class.

clue.text: Quietly heartless proprietor in control

indicators.note: A word's heart is the letter at its centre, and a heartless one has had that middle letter taken out.

parts.note: p is piano on a score, the composer's instruction to play quietly
a proprietor is an owner, five letters whose middle one goes

explanation.surface: A soft-spoken landlord with no feelings at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' means cruel in the surface and means one letter short in the grid, which is the whole of the misdirection. P for quiet comes straight off a sheet of music.
explanation.definitionFit: To have power over something is to have control of it, the two words swapping freely in talk of governments and boards.

clue.text: Positive, possessed by unadulterated ambition

indicators.note: What is possessed by a thing is held within it, so the letters named first sit inside the word that follows.

parts.note: unadulterated means with nothing else mixed in, which is pure
pos is the everyday short form of positive, the opposite of neg

explanation.surface: A cheerful person gripped by an ambition nobody could object to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Positive' opens the clue looking like a mood and is three letters of shorthand. The comma after it is the only sign that it stands apart from the rest of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's purpose is the aim they are set on, which is what 'ambition' names when it means a goal rather than hunger for success.

clue.text: The plan changed after blow, detained by tiny unwanted thing

indicators.note: Something changed is no longer as it was, so the letters beside the word come out in a different arrangement.
To detain a thing is to keep it inside, so the word before goes within the word after.
What comes after a thing follows it, so the shuffled letters go at the back although the clue writes them first.

parts.note: wee is tiny, a Scottish word long since general
a blow landed is a hit
the seven letters of THE PLAN in a new order

explanation.surface: A scheme rethought after somebody threw a punch.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue writes the shuffled letters first and the grid wants them last, which is the job 'after' is quietly doing. 'The' belongs to the fodder rather than to the grammar of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A white elephant is a possession too costly to keep and too awkward to be rid of, named for the albino elephants a Siamese king gave to ruin courtiers.

clue.text: Dependent on books, supporting storyteller endlessly

indicators.note: A word taken endlessly never reaches its end, so its final letter is left off.
A support sits underneath what it holds up, so in a down clue the books go below the storyteller instead of before them.

parts.note: a book on birds is a book re birds, so 'on' is the two letters meaning concerning
a storyteller in the joking sense is a liar, one letter short here
NT is the New Testament, the books a setter reaches for first

explanation.surface: Somebody who cannot manage without the library, propping up a spinner of tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dependent on' is such a natural pair that the 'on' looks like half the definition, and it is two letters of wordplay. The storyteller wanted here is a liar, not a novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone reliant on a thing cannot do without it, which is exactly what being dependent amounts to.

clue.text: Romeo in foolish lover's action open to question

indicators.note: A fool keeps nothing in its proper place, so the letters beside the word will not stay as they are written.
'in' puts the thing named before it inside the thing named after it, so the single letter goes within the shuffled ones.

parts.note: the twelve letters of LOVER'S ACTION rearranged
R is Romeo in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: Some idiotic thing a suitor did that people are still arguing about.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo is Shakespeare's lover in the surface and a single radio letter in the grid, and the clue drops him in among another lover's letters so both readings sit on the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something controversial is disputed rather than settled, so it stays open to question however long it is argued over.

clue.text: Revolutionary reject, receiving attention, had intense desire

indicators.note: A revolution turns a thing right round, so the word it governs is written the other way about.
To receive a thing is to take it in, so the word doing the receiving is written round what it takes.

parts.note: to reject a claim is to deny it, and the turn sends those four letters backwards
to give a person your ear is to give them your attention

explanation.surface: A rebel turned down for a post, heard out politely, wanting it badly all the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' is a person in the surface and an instruction in the grid, which is the oldest costume in the setter's wardrobe. Lending an ear is where 'attention' gets its three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To have yearned for something is to have wanted it painfully and for a long while, the past tense matching the definition's 'had'.

clue.text: Mostly choose time for musical drama

indicators.note: Most of a word is not all of it, so the last letter is dropped and the rest kept.

parts.note: to choose between things is to opt, here stopping a letter short
an era is a stretch of time with a character of its own

explanation.surface: Nearly picking the evening for a night at the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: Three letters cut to two is the smallest deletion a setter can ask for, and 'mostly' reads as ordinary emphasis. Era is the crossword's first answer whenever time is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: An opera is a drama sung all the way through rather than spoken, so 'musical drama' describes the form exactly.

clue.text: Three-quarters of service all the same

indicators.note: Three quarters of an eight-letter word is six letters counted from the front, so the last two never arrive.

parts.note: evensong is the Anglican evening service, sung towards the end of the day

explanation.surface: Most of the service being much like the rest of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' offers a tennis serve, a car service and a church service, and only the last one runs to eight letters. Counting fractions of a word is rare enough that the phrase reads as plain description.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Even so' concedes the point just made and then sets it aside, which is the job 'all the same' does in a sentence.

clue.text: Look at rising worker, perhaps securing vacancy, finally over everyone

indicators.note: In a down clue what rises is written from the bottom of the entry upwards, so those letters go in backwards.
In a down clue what is over something sits above it, so the letters made so far go in first and the rest hang below.
To secure a thing is to hold it fast inside, so the letters doing the securing close round what follows.

parts.note: a worker is a bee — 'perhaps' marks it as one example of the class — and the climb turns the three letters round

indicators.note: What comes finally comes at the very end, so only the last letter of the word before it is taken.

parts.note: the last letter of VACANCY
everyone means all of them

explanation.surface: An employee on the way up landing the vacant post ahead of everybody else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worker' is the crossword's bee before it is anything else. 'Vacancy' is the post being filled in the surface, and only its final letter ever reaches the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball a thing is to look hard and openly at it, a slangy verb standing in for the verb phrase 'Look at'.

clue.text: Deer, for example, climbing above river, walk unsteadily

indicators.note: In a down clue what climbs is written from the bottom upwards, so the two letters go in the other way round.
In a down clue what stands above something is written before it, so the river ends up at the foot of the entry.

parts.note: a stag is a full-grown male deer
'for example' is eg, and the climb stands those two letters on their head
R is the map-maker's short form for river

explanation.surface: A deer working its way up the bank above a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deer, for example' reads as one phrase marking a species, and the two halves belong to different pieces of wordplay. 'For example' is the letters e and g; 'Deer' on its own is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: To stagger is to walk in lurching, uncertain steps, the way someone dazed or drunk gets across a room.

clue.text: Disclose record about ball

indicators.note: Turning about means facing the other way, so the letters assembled so far are read back to front.

parts.note: to disclose a secret is to tell it
an EP is an extended-play record, longer than a single and shorter than an album

explanation.surface: Giving away what is on an old vinyl disc.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container instruction and is a turn instead; nothing here goes inside anything. All six letters reverse at once rather than one piece at a time.
explanation.definitionFit: A pellet is a small ball of shot, paper or animal feed, the word naming the shape rather than the stuff it is made of.

clue.text: Seem worried about church plan

indicators.note: A worried person cannot settle, and letters that will not settle come out in a different order.
Set about a thing means placed round it, so the shuffled letters close over what follows.

parts.note: the four letters of SEEM in another order
CH is the standard short form of church, as printed on a map

explanation.surface: Looking anxious about the state of the parish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seem worried' is a natural phrase about somebody's face, and only the first word's letters are wanted. Four letters is about the shortest fodder an anagram ever gets.
explanation.definitionFit: A scheme is a worked-out plan, often with something sly about it, though the bare sense is simply a plan.

clue.text: Further part of complex translation

indicators.note: A part of something is taken from inside it, so a run of letters is read straight out of the words that follow.

parts.note: the letters run unbroken across the join between the two words

explanation.surface: A bit more of a difficult translation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of' does double duty: a portion of the work in the surface, a portion of the letters in the grid. The join falls inside both words, where no solver naturally breaks them.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra means over and above what was there already, which is what 'further' means when it counts rather than measures.

clue.text: Police officer consuming hour in helicopter

indicators.note: To consume a thing is to take it inside you, so the word before it is written round what comes after.

parts.note: copper is the long-standing British word for a police officer, shortened to cop
h is the abbreviation for hour, as in 24h

explanation.surface: A policeman eating his lunch aboard a helicopter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Consuming hour' reads as an hour that eats up the day and is an instruction to swallow a single letter. Copper for a policeman comes from 'to cop', meaning to catch.
explanation.definitionFit: Chopper is the everyday slang for a helicopter, taken from the chopping noise the rotor blades make.

clue.text: Love job lacking nothing in colour

indicators.note: What a thing lacks it does not have, so the letter named after the word is struck out of it.

parts.note: love is the tennis score of nothing, written as a nought
a job is a chore, and the nothing it loses is its O

explanation.surface: Being so fond of a task that not a scrap of it gets left out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing' works in both halves of the clue: it is the O at the front and it is the O taken out of the job. 'Love' is that same nought, borrowed from the tennis court.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is the yellow-brown earth pigment, and the word now names the shade as readily as the clay it was ground from.

clue.text: Some require singular substance produced by trees

indicators.note: Some of a thing is only part of it, so a run of letters is taken from inside the words that follow.

parts.note: the letters run unbroken across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A demand for one of something rather than several.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular' is the crossword's usual signal for the letter S, which is exactly why it is here doing nothing of the kind. 'Some' at the head of a clue is worth checking for buried letters every time.
explanation.definitionFit: Resin is the sticky sap that oozes from a cut pine or fir and hardens as it meets the air.

clue.text: Record held by unusually great leaders engaged in dispute

indicators.note: What is done unusually is not done in the usual way, so the letters beside the word are not in their usual order.
A thing held by something is kept inside it, so the word before goes within the letters after.

parts.note: the five letters of GREAT rearranged
a ship's log is the running record kept of a voyage
the leaders of a school or a firm are its heads

explanation.surface: A record held by some exceptionally great leaders who have fallen out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' looks like an achievement the leaders hold and is three letters of wordplay. A loggerhead was a long-handled iron tool, and two of them swung at each other gave English the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people at loggerheads are locked in a quarrel neither will give way on, which is being engaged in dispute.

clue.text: Performer missing first level

indicators.note: What is missing first has lost its opening letter, so the word starts one letter later than it should.

parts.note: a performer on a stage or a pitch is a player

explanation.surface: An entertainer who has missed the opening round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missing first' reads as turning up late in the surface and names a letter's position in the grid. Player covers an actor, a musician and a footballer, so the scene can be any of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A layer is one horizontal level in something stacked — of cake, of rock, of paint — so 'level' names it plainly.

clue.text: Over ten working for club

indicators.note: Something working is in motion, and letters in motion do not stay in the order they are given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: More than ten people on the shift this morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over ten working' reads as a headcount, and the first two words are letters rather than sense. Everton is the Liverpool football club that plays in blue, founded in 1878.
explanation.definitionFit: Everton is an English football club, so 'club' names it by its class rather than describing it.
